newsitem.title: HONG KONG: Hong Kong ponders source of stock rally funds.
newsitem.headline: Hong Kong ponders source of stock rally funds.

text.p: Everybody from punters to strategists in Hong Kong is trying to figure out the source of funds driving the Hang Seng index to spectacular record highs.

Theories abound. The switching of funds among Asian markets, a heady gush of enthusiasm from mainland Chinese investors or sudden foreign inflows from Japan, the United States and Europe -- all take the credit for Hong Kong's stock market fervour.

Hong Kong's key index of 33 blue chip stocks has skyrocketed 1,645 points or 15 percent since early September's level of 10,957, reaching another record intraday high on Wednesday of 12,602, up 111 points from Tuesday's close. On Wednesday, the Hang Seng index closed 94.52 points lower at 12,396.18.
The variety of views suggests nobody can safely pinpoint a primary driving force in the rally.
"None of these opinions are contradictory. It is a combination of all of them," said Daniel Widdicombe, managing director at Bear Stearns Asia Ltd.

Widdicombe cited specific orders to back up his view that U.S. funds are entering Hong Kong on fears that U.S. earnings growth has peaked and that the Dow Jones Industrial Average has topped out following its recent high of 6,043.92.
But the head trader at another U.S. brokerage said he had seen virtually no U.S. money coming into the territory.
"It doesn't appear to be coming from the U.S," he said. "It's embarrassing. I've spoken to other people and we haven't seen the business you might think we'd see at the moment."

The same is true of Japanese flows. An analyst at a Japanese broker said he witnessed heavy Japanese demand for Hong Kong stocks. "There is clearly a capital outflow taking place from Japan," agreed Clive McDonnell, economist at Crosby Financial.
But Marshall Mays at Nikko Research Centre (Hong Kong) Ltd said there have been no major flows from Japan into Hong Kong.
"I haven't seen any reallocation away from Japan in the last couple of months," he said.
While views vary widely on the contribution foreign flows are making to the rally, many market watchers agree that switching between Asian markets is also having an impact.
Funds are leaving the battered bourses of Thailand and, to a lesser extent Singapore and the Philippines, in favour of better returns in Hong Kong, they said.

"I don't think there's any real new money to the region. I think to quite a large extent there has been asset reallocation within regional funds," said Stephen Leung, chief investment officer at BZW Asia.
However, the Hang Seng index suddenly roared higher on October 9, October 14 and October 15 just as London opened, suggesting that European investors are buying Hong Kong stocks aggressively.

Many foreign brokers based in Hong Kong also said names of Chinese brokers were popping up frequently on electronic trading screens, suggesting that mainland Chinese money could be entering the Hong Kong market through local brokers. "I think it's mainland money," said one U.S. broker.
But at least one Chinese broker rejected that idea. "I temporarily don't see the so-called China funds in the market," said Patrick Chia of China Everbright Securities.
Chinese investors are known to have bought red chips, or China-backed local companies, recently and are expected to continue doing so in the future.

Widdicombe said the variety of views confirmed that funds entering Hong Kong were broadly-based. "If you're working in a Japanese or a U.K. company you will see more order flow from your own market and client base," he said. "I think it's all these factors in tandem."
